enonce_markdown: Which event takes place during the rising phase (depolarisation) of an action potential in an axon?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

An action potential is produced by two successive changes in membrane permeability: first to sodium ions (the inside becomes positive), then to potassium ions (the inside becomes negative again).

### Solution

When the threshold is reached, **voltage-gated sodium channels open** and $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions diffuse into the axon down their electrochemical gradient. The positive charge entering reverses the potential across the membrane from about $-70\ \mathrm{mV}$ to about $+40\ \mathrm{mV}$.

- Potassium channels open later and cause repolarisation, as $\mathrm{K^+}$ leaves.
- The sodium-potassium pump removes $3\ \mathrm{Na^+}$ and brings in $2\ \mathrm{K^+}$, it is not the cause of the rapid rise and moves sodium out of the axon, not in.
- Chloride ions do not cause the depolarisation of an axon.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: Voltage-gated potassium channels open and potassium ions diffuse out of the axon
The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions into the axon
Chloride ions diffuse into the axon through open channels
Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions diffuse into the axon

enonce_markdown: Which statement explains why an action potential travels faster along a myelinated axon than along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Myelin is an electrical insulator. Where it covers the membrane no ions cross, so the depolarisation can only be regenerated at the gaps, the nodes of Ranvier: this is saltatory conduction.

### Solution

The myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells prevents ion movement across the membrane except at the **nodes of Ranvier**, where the voltage-gated channels are concentrated. Local currents flow along the inside of the axon from one node to the next and bring the next node to threshold, so the impulse **jumps from node to node**. Fewer regions have to be depolarised, so conduction is faster and less ATP is needed to pump the ions back.

- Myelin does not speed up diffusion of ions through the membrane, it blocks it.
- Schwann cells do not pump sodium along the axon.
- Voltage-gated channels are not found all along a myelinated axon, they are concentrated at the nodes.

**Answer: a.**

choix.texte: Local currents carry the depolarisation from one node of Ranvier to the next, so the impulse jumps between nodes
The myelin sheath makes ions diffuse faster through the membrane of the axon
Schwann cells pump sodium ions along the length of the axon
Voltage-gated channels are present along the whole length of the myelinated membrane

enonce_markdown:
A student stimulates a myelinated motor axon at one point and records the action potential at a second point $0.45\ \mathrm{m}$ further along the axon. The impulse reaches the second point $6.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ after the stimulus.

Calculate the speed of conduction of the impulse.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Speed $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. Convert the time to seconds first: $1\ \mathrm{ms} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

### Solution

Time: $6.0\ \mathrm{ms} = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

$$v = \frac{0.45\ \mathrm{m}}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}} = 75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

This is a typical value for a myelinated axon.

- $0.075\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: the time in milliseconds was used as if it were in seconds.
- $13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: time was divided by distance instead of distance by time.
- $270\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: the value in $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ was written with the unit $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

**Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: An action potential reaches the presynaptic knob of a cholinergic synapse. Which row correctly gives the sequence of events that follows?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Synaptic transmission is chemical: the electrical signal is converted into the release of a neurotransmitter, which crosses the cleft by diffusion and triggers a new depolarisation in the postsynaptic membrane.

### Solution

The depolarisation of the presynaptic membrane opens **voltage-gated $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ channels**. $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ions diffuse in, which causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release **acetylcholine** by exocytosis. It diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium channels and so depolarising it. This one-way sequence is why a synapse conducts in one direction only.

- Acetylcholine is released from the presynaptic neurone, it does not diffuse back to the presynaptic membrane.
- Sodium channels in the postsynaptic membrane open after, not before, the neurotransmitter binds.
- Acetylcholine is removed by acetylcholinesterase, not by being stored in the cleft.

**Answer: b.**

choix.texte: Acetylcholine diffuses from the postsynaptic membrane to the presynaptic membrane and opens calcium channels
Calcium channels open and calcium ions enter, vesicles fuse with the membrane and acetylcholine is released into the cleft
Sodium channels open in the postsynaptic membrane, then acetylcholine is released from the presynaptic knob
Acetylcholine accumulates in the cleft and the presynaptic knob stops releasing it after one impulse

enonce_markdown:
Tetrodotoxin, a poison found in the pufferfish, binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels. A giant axon is placed in a solution containing the poison and is then stimulated electrically.

Explain the effect of the poison on (a) the resting potential and (b) the action potential. *[5 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Separate what sets the resting potential (the sodium-potassium pump and the leakage of $\mathrm{K^+}$ through open channels) from what produces the action potential (the opening of voltage-gated $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels).

### Solution

**(a) Resting potential.** It is **not changed (or hardly changed)**. It depends mainly on the **sodium-potassium pump** ($3\ \mathrm{Na^+}$ out, $2\ \mathrm{K^+}$ in) and on the much greater permeability of the membrane to $\mathrm{K^+}$ through leak channels, which are not the voltage-gated sodium channels blocked by the poison.

**(b) Action potential.** It is **abolished**. The stimulus cannot open the voltage-gated sodium channels, which are blocked, so $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions cannot rush into the axon. The membrane cannot be depolarised to the threshold and the inside never becomes positive (about $+40\ \mathrm{mV}$). With no action potential there is no nerve impulse to conduct along the axon (and none to reach a synapse), so the poison causes paralysis.

enonce_markdown:
A squid giant axon is bathed in sea water, and its action potential is recorded. The axon is then placed in a solution in which the concentration of sodium ions is half that of sea water, with every other ion unchanged.

Which row correctly predicts the effects on the resting potential and on the action potential in the axon?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The size of an action potential depends on the electrochemical gradient for $\mathrm{Na^+}$, because the rising phase is made by $\mathrm{Na^+}$ entering. The resting potential depends mostly on $\mathrm{K^+}$, since the resting membrane is only slightly permeable to $\mathrm{Na^+}$.

### Solution

Lowering the outside concentration of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ reduces the electrochemical gradient driving $\mathrm{Na^+}$ inwards. When the sodium channels open, **less sodium enters**, so the rise of the potential is slower and the **peak of the action potential is lower** (less positive). The resting membrane is only slightly permeable to $\mathrm{Na^+}$, so the **resting potential is almost unchanged**.

- The resting potential would change greatly only if the concentration of $\mathrm{K^+}$ were altered.
- The action potential does not stay the same, because it depends on the entry of $\mathrm{Na^+}$, and the pump does not keep the outside concentration at the original value in a bathing solution.
- With some sodium still present an action potential is produced; it does not disappear.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: The resting potential becomes much more negative and the action potential is unchanged
The resting potential and the action potential are both unchanged, because the pump keeps the gradient constant
The resting potential becomes zero and no action potential can be produced
The resting potential is almost unchanged and the peak of the action potential is lower
